chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abdullah, from Ali ibn Ja'far, who said:

I heard Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him) saying: 'When his believing brother comes to him with a need, it is but a mercy from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that has been conveyed to him. If he accepts that need, he has connected it with our Wilayah, and he is connected with the Wilayah of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.'

And if he repels him from his need while he is able to fulfill it, Allah will cause a serpent of fire to gnaw him in his grave until the Day of Judgment. He will be either forgiven or punished; and if the seeker excuses him, his state will be worse.

He said: 'And I heard him saying: Whoever a man from his brethren approaches seeking refuge/help from him in one of his states, and he does not grant him refuge after being able to do so, he has cut off the Wilayah of Allah, Blessed and High.'

key_terms.شُجَاعاً مِنْ نَارٍ: A serpent or beast of fire

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual consequence of rejecting a believing brother's need according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) links the social act of fulfilling a believer's need directly to theological status, framing it as an extension of divine mercy and a tangible connection to the Wilayah of the Imams. The hadith provides a stark eschatological warning for those who reject such pleas despite having the capacity, describing a specific punishment of being gnawed by a 'serpent of fire' in the grave, while also noting that the petitioner's excuse can mitigate this severity. This underscores the Shia concept of 'Wilayah' not just as spiritual authority, but as a relational bond maintained through mutual support among the faithful.
